newsitem.title: UK: London Forex staff cuts seen continuing.
newsitem.headline: London Forex staff cuts seen continuing.

text.p: Cuts in foreign exchange staffing seen recently in some London trading rooms are unlikely to be the last as currency markets adjust to major changes in the trading environment, analysts said on Friday.
Relatively low volatility, tightening bid/ask spreads, the growth of electronic trading and an overall drive for greater efficiency is forcing many particpants to reassess their dealing operations.

"There is a feeling that we are at a watershed," said Chris Sadler, corporate sales trader at Hambros Bank in London. "Central banks seem to have rates under control and with rates stable there is gradually less volatility and less opportunities for banks to make money."

While global forex turnover is still expected to grow, greater transparency and liquidity has seen bid/ask spreads tighten to a degree where only the largest participants can achieve an economy of scale between turnover and costs that can sustain a profit.
And as these markets mature, liquidity is migrating increasingly to only a handful of major players.

According the Bank for International Settlements' (BIS) latest forex survey, the 10 most active banks in London had increased their market share by one percent to 44 percent by 1995 from 1992, a figure many see growing substantially in the coming years.

Electronic broking has also made an impact with smaller orders being executed this way more cheaply and efficiently. The same BIS survey showed that electronic broking systems accounted for five percent of London turnover in 1995.

While this ultimately benefits the end-user by bringing cheaper dealing costs, it comes at the expense of a role previously filled by the traditional voice broker and has virtually sealed the fate of the so-called metro, or small order desk.
Few have been surprised by these trends which started to accelerate early in the year and almost nobody expects a return to the heady days of the forex boom of the early 1990s.

Speaking at foreign exchange conference this summer, Albert Maasland, head of continental Europe forex sales and trading at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said: "The industry is moving to fewer people with higher qualifications. Basically, if you can't add value, your role has disappeared."
Foreign exchange jobs are still there, but fewer trading and broking jobs are being created.

"People are uncertain about what's going to happen especially with what a single European currency will bring," said one London forex recruitment specialist. "But there will always be a foreign exchange market, we just won't see the demand for the G7 trader anymore."
The onset of Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) will inevitably hit forex staffing levels.

"When EMU does come along, you'll see the disappearance of five to six active currencies," said Hambros' Sadler. "We're getting more clients than ever before, we're getting the volume, but we're also getting a contraction in the amount of instruments to trade."
The start of EMU may prompt a migration to niche markets such as emerging market currencies. But competition is getting fierce here too, and desks are generally smaller.
Industry optimists see the current lack of volatility and relative global stability as merely a cyclical trough and anticipate a return to more volatile, and profitable, times.

"All this doom and gloom is music to my ears," said one proprietary trader. "Historically, it usually indicates that something is about to happen. Some might see this as a good time to get into the market rather than get out."
